name: static int enable_%%MODEL_NAME%%(void)
prose: Generated function enable_%%MODEL_NAME%% (template tools/verification/rvgen/rvgen/templates/ltl2k/main.c, lines 57-68), where %%MODEL_NAME%% is replaced by the model name when a monitor is generated; it is the .enable callback of the monitor's struct rv_monitor and takes no parameters. It calls ltl_monitor_init(); if that returns nonzero the function returns that value at once, before the %%TRACEPOINT_ATTACH%% placeholder is expanded, so no tracepoint probe of this function is attached. ltl_monitor_init (include/rv/ltl_monitor.h) gets a task monitor slot (returning its negative error if that fails), attaches a probe on task_newtask, and initialises the LTL monitor state of every existing thread and each present CPU's idle task. On success the function expands the generated tracepoint-attach code (whatever %%TRACEPOINT_ATTACH%% becomes) and returns 0; the matching disable function detaches the tracepoints and calls ltl_monitor_destroy().
note: Name is the template function head as it appears in the file. Reviewer round 15 (formal contract only constrains the return sign and omits attaching and disable ownership) right as a criticism of the contract, which is removed (the function touches kernel global state and generated code). The old prose omitted that ltl_monitor_init itself attaches a task_newtask probe. Tally 1 right 0 wrong.

name: static int __init register_%%MODEL_NAME%%(void)
prose: Generated function register_%%MODEL_NAME%% (template ltl2k/main.c lines 87-90), the module init function (module_init) of a generated monitor, with no parameters. It returns rv_register_monitor(&rv_%%MODEL_NAME%%, %%PARENT%%), where %%PARENT%% is substituted by the generator (a parent monitor pointer or NULL). rv_register_monitor returns -EINVAL if the monitor name is too long or if the parent is itself a nested monitor, -EEXIST if a monitor of the same name is already registered, the error of create_monitor_dir if creating the monitor's directory fails, and 0 after adding the monitor to the monitor list; it takes and releases rv_interface_lock internally. On a nonzero return the monitor is not added to the list, although monitor->parent may already have been set. After a successful return the module's exit function unregister_%%MODEL_NAME%% calls rv_unregister_monitor.
note: Name is the template function head. Reviewer round 15 (formal contract omits the registration side effect and unregister ownership) right as a criticism of the contract, which is removed. Checked rv_register_monitor in kernel/trace/rv/rv.c:776-819. Tally 1 right 0 wrong.

name: used_empty
prose: Function used_empty() in virtio_ring_0_9.c (lines 197-208) returns bool and only reads state. It reads guest.last_used_idx (and, under RING_POLL, ring.used->ring[last_used_idx & (ring_size - 1)].id). Without RING_POLL it returns ring.used->idx == guest.last_used_idx, true when the host has published no used entry beyond last_used_idx. Under RING_POLL it returns the expression (id ^ last_used_idx ^ 0x8000) & ~(ring_size - 1) converted to bool, so it is true when that expression is nonzero (the id field at the slot does not carry the expected high bits and thus no new used entry is visible there) and false when it is zero. It requires the ring to have been set up by alloc_ring.
note: Reviewers: round 1 (contract omits the initialisation precondition) moot, contract removed; round 2 (ignores the RING_POLL branch) right; round 15 (RING_POLL returns true when the high-bit expression is nonzero, not zero as the prose said) right (virtio_ring_0_9.c:204). Tally 2 right 0 wrong.

name: enable_call
prose: Function enable_call() in virtio_ring_0_9.c (lines 217-224), returns bool. It stores guest.last_used_idx into vring_used_event(&ring), which the virtio ring header defines as ring.avail->ring[ring.num] (the used-event slot at the end of the available ring, not a field of the used ring), executes smp_mb(), and returns used_empty(). So the return value is true when no used entry beyond last_used_idx is visible after the store (ring.used->idx == last_used_idx without RING_POLL, or, under RING_POLL, the used_empty expression (id ^ last_used_idx ^ 0x8000) & ~(ring_size - 1) being nonzero), and false when a new used entry is already available. It requires the ring to have been set up by alloc_ring.
note: Reviewers: round 1 (omits the used_event write and barrier) right; round 2 (the return under RING_POLL is not used->idx equality) right; round 15 (inherits the RING_POLL polarity error of used_empty: true when nonzero, not zero) right (virtio_ring_0_9.c:197-224; vring_used_event defined at include/uapi/linux/virtio_ring.h:196). Tally 3 right 0 wrong.

name: kvm_vm_set_mem_attributes
prose: Static function kvm_vm_set_mem_attributes(kvm, start, end, attributes) in virt/kvm/kvm_main.c (lines 2566-2627), compiled under CONFIG_KVM_GENERIC_MEMORY_ATTRIBUTES. The caller must not hold kvm->slots_lock. It builds the xarray entry (xa_mk_value(attributes), or NULL when attributes is 0), emits a tracepoint, takes kvm->slots_lock and releases it at out_unlock on every path (there is no early return). If kvm_range_has_memory_attributes(kvm, start, end, ~0, attributes) says the whole range already has the wanted attributes it jumps to out_unlock and returns 0 without any invalidation or xarray change. Otherwise it calls xa_reserve(&kvm->mem_attr_array, i, GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT) for every index in [start, end); a failure goes to out_unlock and returns that error (r), with the reservations already made for lower indices left in the array and no invalidation phase run. Next it runs kvm_handle_gfn_range with the pre-set range (invalidation begin under the MMU lock, kvm_pre_set_memory_attributes adds the range and calls the arch hook, remote TLBs are flushed if a handler returned true), then calls xa_store for every index with KVM_BUG_ON(r, kvm) on the xa_err result (r is overwritten by each iteration, so the value returned is that of the last xa_store), then runs the post-set range (kvm_arch_post_set_memory_attributes, invalidation end), and returns r (0 unless the last store failed).
note: Reviewers: original (the no-op path returns 0 without running invalidation phases) right (kvm_main.c:2596-2598); round 15 (on xa_reserve failure earlier reservations may remain, so the xarray is not unchanged) right (lines 2604-2610). The old prose also said xa_store failures 'do not return'; r from the last store is what is returned. Tally 2 right 0 wrong. Whole function read (plus kvm_handle_gfn_range).

name: kvm_vcpu_halt
prose: Function kvm_vcpu_halt(vcpu) in virt/kvm/kvm_main.c (lines 3750-3820), returns nothing; vcpu must be a vCPU of the calling task. It computes max_halt_poll_ns with kvm_vcpu_max_halt_poll_ns (the VM's max_halt_poll_ns when override_halt_poll_ns is set, else the module parameter halt_poll_ns) and halt_poll_allowed = !kvm_arch_no_poll(vcpu); it clamps vcpu->halt_poll_ns to max_halt_poll_ns (also when polling is not allowed); polling is done when halt_poll_allowed and vcpu->halt_poll_ns is nonzero. When polling it loops over kvm_vcpu_check_block(vcpu) (a negative result, meaning the vCPU is runnable, has a pending timer, a signal is pending, or a KVM_REQ_UNBLOCK request was consumed) until kvm_vcpu_can_poll says stop; if a wake condition is found during the poll it skips blocking and goes straight to the statistics. Otherwise it calls kvm_vcpu_block(vcpu), which blocks until the same check says wake (it returns whether it actually scheduled; if the condition is already true it can return without waiting), and, if it waited, adds the wait time to halt_wait_ns and its histogram. It then computes halt_ns (total time since the start); if polling was done it calls update_halt_poll_stats(vcpu, start, poll_end, !waited). If polling is allowed it re-reads the maximum and: if the wakeup was not valid it shrinks halt_poll_ns (shrink_halt_poll_ns); else if the maximum is nonzero it leaves halt_poll_ns unchanged when halt_ns <= halt_poll_ns, shrinks it when it is nonzero and halt_ns > maximum, grows it (grow_halt_poll_ns) when halt_poll_ns < maximum and halt_ns < maximum; else (maximum 0) sets halt_poll_ns to 0. Finally on every path it calls trace_kvm_vcpu_wakeup(halt_ns, waited, vcpu_valid_wakeup(vcpu)); the grow and shrink helpers have their own tracepoints.
note: Reviewers: original (may return immediately without waiting or polling if a wake condition is already pending) right; round 15 (claims the kvm_vcpu_wakeup tracepoint is updated but the code only has halt-poll grow/shrink tracepoints) wrong: trace_kvm_vcpu_wakeup is called unconditionally at kvm_main.c:3819. Tally 1 right 1 wrong. The whole function was read.

name: do_exchange
prose: Static function do_exchange(cname, argc, argv) in chio.c (lines 252-358); argv[0] is the command name, which it skips, so the argument counts below exclude it. If fewer than 4 or more than 8 arguments follow, it prints a warnx message ("too few" or "too many arguments") and then a usage message to stderr and returns 1. Otherwise it zeroes a struct changer_exchange and parses: the source element type with parse_element_type (an unknown name calls errx(1, ...)); if the source type is the voltag pseudo type CHET_VT it resolves the next argument with find_element, otherwise it parses the next argument as a unit number with parse_element_unit (negative or non-numeric calls errx(1, ...)); the same for dst1 (so a voltag is allowed for the source and for the first destination). If no more arguments remain or the next one is a special word, the second destination is set equal to the source; otherwise it parses a dst2 type (CHET_VT there calls errx(1, "voltag only makes sense as an element source")) and then reads the next argument as the dst2 unit with parse_element_unit without checking that an argument remains. Remaining arguments are modifiers parsed with parse_special (unknown words call errx(1, ...)); inv1 sets CE_INVERT1, inv2 sets CE_INVERT2, any other special word calls errx(1, "inappropriate modifier"). It then calls ioctl(changer_fd, CHIOEXCHANGE, &cmd); failure calls err(1, ...). It returns 0 after a successful ioctl. The err/errx exits are not returns.
note: Reviewer round 15 (the annotation says a voltag is invalid as any destination, but the code allows it for dst1) right (chio.c:294-296, 317-319); the old prose also said an invalid argument terminates but did not say which. I also noted that the dst2 unit is parsed without checking that an argument is left (chio.c:314-322). Tally 1 right 0 wrong. The whole function was read.

name: read_stream
prose: Function read_stream(fp, n) in ed/io.c (lines 72-112), returns long (ERR on failure). fp is an open stream and n a valid line address (0..addr_last). It finds the line node at n, remembers the old newline_added and isbinary values and whether n == addr_last (appended), clears isbinary and newline_added, sets current_addr = n, and repeatedly calls get_stream_line(fp) while it returns a positive length; each line is stored with put_sbuf_line and linked after the previous one, the first line pushes an UADD undo record starting at current_addr and later lines extend its end pointer, and size accumulates the returned lengths. Failures: put_sbuf_line returning NULL, or push_undo_stack returning NULL, make it return ERR at once (isbinary and newline_added keep the values set during the read, not the saved ones); get_stream_line returning a negative value (read error or out of memory) also returns ERR. On normal end of input: if it was an append to the end and the old and new state were binary with a newline added it prints "newline inserted" to stderr, otherwise if a newline was added (and either not appending or neither the old nor the new data was binary) it prints "newline appended"; if the data was binary, a newline was added and it was not an append, size is incremented by 1; if size is 0, newline_added is set to 1; newline_added is then kept only when appending (otherwise restored to the old value), isbinary is OR-ed with its old value, and size is returned. When the stream yields no lines, no undo record is pushed and current_addr is left equal to n.
note: Reviewers: original (says lines appended before address n; code appends after n) right as a criticism of that wording, and the old prose here already said 'after line n'; round 15 (success on an empty stream pushes no undo record and does not advance current_addr) right (io.c:83-98). The old prose said it always 'pushed an undo record, advanced current_addr' on success. Tally 2 right 0 wrong.

name: get_tty_line
prose: Function get_tty_line() in ed/io.c (lines 261-297), no parameters; it reads from stdin with getchar into the module's growable buffer ibuf (size ibufsz, which may start as NULL and 0, grown by the REALLOC macro). For each character other than EOF it resets oi to 0, makes room for i + 2 bytes, stores the character (a NUL byte sets isbinary = 1) and, if the character is not a newline, continues. On a newline it increments lineno, stores '\0' after it, sets ibufp = ibuf and returns i, the number of bytes stored including the newline. On EOF: if ferror(stdin) it prints a message, sets errmsg = "cannot read stdin", clears the error with clearerr, sets ibufp = NULL and returns ERR. Otherwise it clears the EOF state with clearerr and, if bytes were stored since the last EOF (i != oi), sets oi = i and reads on (so a second getchar is attempted after a first EOF with partial data); if no new byte arrived it stores '\0' after the data when i is nonzero, sets ibufp = ibuf and returns i, which is 0 for immediate EOF (then no NUL is written, lineno and isbinary are unchanged, and ibufp = ibuf, which is NULL if ibuf was never allocated) and the partial line length otherwise (lineno is not incremented for such a line without a trailing newline). If REALLOC fails (realloc returns NULL) it prints strerror to stderr, sets errmsg = "out of memory" and returns ERR; ibuf and ibufsz keep their old values and ibufp is not changed by this function.
note: Reviewers: round 1 (on immediate EOF returning 0 the code does not set ibuf[0] to NUL) right (io.c:288-294); round 2 (ERR can also result from REALLOC failure) right; round 15 (REALLOC failure sets errmsg, contrary to the annotation's no errmsg change) right (ed.h:139-149 REALLOC sets errmsg = "out of memory"). The old prose said no errmsg change by this function on REALLOC failure. Tally 3 right 0 wrong.

name: extract_addr_range
prose: Function extract_addr_range() in ed/main.c (lines 243-261), no parameters, returns int. It works on the command buffer at ibufp and the globals first_addr, second_addr, addr_cnt and current_addr. It sets addr_cnt = 0 and first_addr = second_addr = current_addr, then repeatedly calls next_addr() while it returns a non-negative address (next_addr returns EOF when there is no address at ibufp and ERR on an error; for a leading ',', '%' or ';' next_addr itself also changes addr_cnt and second_addr). For each address it increments addr_cnt, sets first_addr = second_addr and second_addr = the new address; if *ibufp is neither ',' nor ';' the loop stops (leaving ibufp at that character), otherwise it consumes the separator and, for ';', sets current_addr to the address just parsed. After the loop addr_cnt is capped at 2; if addr_cnt equals 1, or if the loop ended because next_addr returned a negative value (EOF or ERR, which is always different from second_addr), first_addr is set equal to second_addr. So with exactly one address both are that address; with two or more addresses and the loop ended by a non-separator character, first_addr and second_addr are the last two addresses; but when a separator was followed by no valid address (EOF or ERR), first_addr and second_addr both equal the last parsed address (or current_addr if none was parsed). It returns ERR when the last next_addr call returned ERR, and 0 otherwise (including when it stopped with EOF). It allocates and frees nothing.
note: Reviewers: round 2 (says one parsed address defaults both to current_addr; code sets both to that address) right as a criticism of that wording, and the old prose here already said 'both to the single parsed address'; round 15 (after an error or end following a separator, first_addr is set to second_addr, not the last two parsed addresses) right (main.c:258-259); the old prose said 'the last two parsed addresses'. Round 1 (contract weaker than prose) moot. Tally 2 right 0 wrong. Checked next_addr (main.c:275-348) for its return values.

name: exec_command
prose: Function exec_command() in ed/main.c (lines 427-852), no parameters, returns int; it executes one command from the command buffer at ibufp, using the globals first_addr, second_addr, addr_cnt, current_addr, addr_last, isglobal, modified, scripted and file-static pat, sgflag and sgnum, and its comment says it returns the print request, if any. Return values: ERR (-2) when a command fails (errmsg describes it); EMOD (-3) from 'e' when modified && !scripted (returned immediately), and for 'q' (and 'wq' with the 'q' suffix) when the buffer is modified and not scripted; FATAL (-4), returned only by 'e'/'E' when open_sbuf() fails after the buffer was closed; EOF (-1) for 'Q', for 'q' on an unmodified or scripted session, and for 'wq'/'wQ' as described below; and otherwise gflag at the end of the switch, which is 0 or a set of print flags (GPR 002, GLS 004, GNP 010) collected by the command suffix, for the caller to print (the commands p, n, l and z reset gflag to 0 after displaying). The macro GET_COMMAND_SUFFIX accepts any run of the letters p, l, n (setting those flags in gflag) and then requires a newline, which it consumes, otherwise errmsg = "invalid command suffix" and ERR is returned. After skipping blanks the command letter is read: c, d, j, l, m, n, p, s and t call check_addr_range first (z and the empty command call it with their own bounds; i and k instead reject a second address of 0 with "invalid address"), and a, c, d, i, j, m, s, t read the suffix, clear the undo stack unless isglobal (k and the printing commands do not clear it), and then run append_lines, delete_lines (c also appends at current_addr), join_lines, mark_line_node, display_lines, move_lines (m, after GET_THIRD_ADDR and an 'invalid destination' check), copy_lines, search_and_replace (s, after the suffix parsing of g, p, r and a count, compiling the pattern with get_compiled_pattern and extract_subst_tail, with 'no previous substitution' and 'invalid pattern delimiter' errors), each returning ERR if that helper returns negative (d also sets current_addr to INC_MOD(current_addr, addr_last) when that is nonzero). e/E (addr_cnt must be 0, the next char must be blank, get_filename must succeed) delete all lines, clear undo, close and reopen the buffer (close failure ERR, open failure FATAL), set old_filename, read_file the file (failure ERR) and then clear undo, set modified = 0 and u_current_addr = u_addr_last = -1. f prints the file name (a '!' name is 'invalid redirection'). g, v, G, V reject nesting ('cannot nest global commands'), check the range 1..addr_last, build the active list, increment isglobal and call exec_global (failure ERR). h and H print or toggle the last error message; P toggles the prompt; u pops the undo stack; x always sets errmsg = "crypt unavailable" and returns ERR; = prints addr_last or second_addr; ! runs the shell command with system() and prints '!' unless scripted; r reads a file after second_addr (a positive count not equal to addr_last sets modified = 1); w and W write first_addr..second_addr with write_file ("w" or "a" mode), set modified = 0 when the whole buffer of a non-'!' file was written, with 'q'/'Q' suffix gflag = EOF (or EMOD for 'wq' when still modified and not scripted); an empty command line (newline) prints the next line; any other letter sets errmsg = "unknown command" and returns ERR. Commands that take no address (e, E, f, h, H, P, q, Q, u, x, !) set 'unexpected address' and return ERR when addr_cnt > 0.
note: Reviewer round 15 (formal contract omits the ibufp/state precondition and allows FATAL -3 though never returned) mixed: the contract is removed; FATAL is returned (by 'e'/'E', main.c:487-488) but its value is -4, not -3 (ed.h:38-40: ERR -2, EMOD -3, FATAL -4); the old prose had EMOD -4 and FATAL -3, both wrong, and returned only 0 on success although print-request flags can be returned. Tally 0 right 0 wrong, 1 mixed. The whole function was read.

name: main
prose: main(argc, argv) of getfacl.c (lines 222-287; the slice showed only its tail). It starts with type = ACL_TYPE_ACCESS and the flags h, i, n, q, s, v cleared, and parses options with getopt_long("+dhinqsv", long_options): d sets type = ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT, h, i, n, q, s, v set their flags; any other result calls usage() (which only prints the usage text to stderr and returns) and then main returns -1. After the options, with no operands it calls print_acl_from_stdin and returns 1 if that returned nonzero, else 0. With operands it processes each in order: "-" calls print_acl_from_stdin, any other operand calls print_acl; each result of -1 is remembered, and main returns 1 if any call returned -1 and 0 otherwise. It also has external effects through those helpers: print_acl and print_acl_from_stdin read ACLs, write the ACL text and headers to stdout, write warnings to stderr and read stdin; main itself keeps only local state (the flags, type and the adjusted argc/argv).
note: Reviewer round 15 (the prose says only local state changes, but print_acl/print_acl_from_stdin produce output side effects) right (getfacl.c:164-166, 194, 209-216). The old prose also treated usage() as if it might not return; here it returns and main then returns -1. Tally 1 right 0 wrong.

name: main
prose: main(argc, argv) of ls.c (lines 231-640; the slice showed the middle). It calls setlocale(LC_ALL, ""). If stdout is a terminal it sets termwidth to 80 and replaces it with the numeric value of COLUMNS (parsed with strtonum in [0, INT_MAX]) when COLUMNS is set and not empty, otherwise with the terminal width from TIOCGWINSZ when that succeeds and is positive, and turns on f_nonprint; if stdout is not a terminal it sets f_singlecol and, when COLUMNS is set, parses it the same way. If the COLUMNS value does not parse, termwidth is set back to 80 (an invalid COLUMNS is therefore not an error). It sets fts_options = FTS_PHYSICAL, f_samesort when LS_SAMESORT is set, and (with COLORLS) colorflag = COLORFLAG_AUTO when CLICOLOR is set. It then processes options with getopt_long("+1ABCD:FGHILPRSTUWXZabcdfghiklmnopqrstuvwxy,", long_opts); later options override earlier ones within the groups described in the code (-1/-C/-l/-x, -c/-u/-U, -S/-t/-v, -d versus -R, and so on); -G sets CLICOLOR in the environment and colorflag to AUTO; the --group-directories option accepts 'first' (or no value) and 'last' and otherwise calls errx(2, ...); the --color option accepts the always, auto, never values (no value means always) and otherwise calls errx(2, ...), and without COLORLS it only warns and falls into the default case; an unknown option ('?' or default) calls usage(), which prints a usage message and exits with status 1. After the options it makes -A automatic for uid 0 unless -I, sets up terminal colours from TERM and the termcap entry (and LSCOLORS) when colour is enabled, adds FTS_NOSTAT when no option needs stat information (and colour is off), adds FTS_COMFOLLOW under the stated conditions, adds FTS_WHITEOUT for -W, computes blocksize for -i, -l, -s, selects sortfcn from the sort flags and reverse flag, selects printfcn (printscol, printlong, printstream or printcol), and calls traverse() on the operands, or on "." when there are none, and ends with exit(rval), so it does not return to its caller.
note: Reviewer round 15 (invalid COLUMNS is defaulted to 80, not required to be a valid integer) right (ls.c:263-264); the old prose said it requires COLUMNS be a decimal integer. Also the old prose said an unknown option terminates with status 2 through usage(); usage() exits with status 1 (util.c:227), while the errx(2, ...) paths use status 2. Tally 1 right 0 wrong. The whole function was read.

name: static void aclmode(char *buf, const FTSENT *p)
prose: Function aclmode(buf, p) in ls/print.c (lines 774-838; the slice began in the middle of it), static, returns nothing; it may set buf[10] to '+' for an entry that has a non-trivial ACL (buf must have at least 11 bytes). It keeps three function-level statics: previous_dev (initially NODEV), supports_acls (initially -1) and type (initially ACL_TYPE_ACCESS). It returns without touching buf when p->fts_statp is a character device, block device or whiteout, or when the entry is on previous_dev and supports_acls is 0. It builds name as fts_name for a root-level entry or "<parent fts_accpath>/<fts_name>" otherwise (truncated to the buffer). When the device differs from previous_dev it records the new device, sets supports_acls = 0 and probes with lpathconf(name, _PC_ACL_NFS4): a positive result selects ACL_TYPE_NFS4 and supports_acls = 1; a negative result with errno other than EINVAL prints a warning and returns (previous_dev stays updated and supports_acls stays 0, so later entries on that device return early); if still unsupported it probes _PC_ACL_EXTENDED the same way (positive selects ACL_TYPE_ACCESS). If supports_acls is 0 afterwards it returns. Otherwise it calls acl_get_link_np(name, type); NULL prints a warning and returns; then acl_is_trivial_np(facl, &trivial): a nonzero result frees the ACL, prints a warning and returns; otherwise buf[10] = '+' is set when the ACL is not trivial, and acl_free(facl) is called. Every path that obtained an acl_t frees it.
note: Old record was dropped because the slice had no head; the function is aclmode at print.c:774, so fixed under its real name. No reviewer claim (mechanical rejections only). Checked every return in lines 774-838.

name: list
prose: Function list() in pax/ar_subs.c (lines 67-135), no parameters, returns nothing; it lists the archive members that match the user's patterns. It first calls get_arc() (which sets the global format pointer frmt), then (*frmt->options)() and (*frmt->st_rd)(), and returns immediately if any is negative; with vflag it also starts the uid/gid caches with uidtb_start() and gidtb_start() and returns immediately if either fails. These early returns leave the archive open and do not call pat_chk. Otherwise it takes now = time(NULL) and loops while next_head(arcn) returns 0: pat_match(arcn) < 0 ends the loop; if pat_match returned 0 and sel_chk(arcn) is 0 the member is selected: pat_sel(arcn) < 0 ends the loop, mod_name(arcn) < 0 ends the loop, and ls_list(arcn, now, stdout) is called only when mod_name returned 0 (a positive result skips the listing); then, for every member whether selected or not, rd_skip(arcn->skip + arcn->pad) is called and a result of 1 ends the loop. After the loop it calls (*frmt->end_rd)() (result ignored), blocks signals with sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &s_mask, NULL), calls ar_close() and then pat_chk().
note: Reviewers: original (frmt is initialised by get_arc, not by the caller; early returns skip ar_close/pat_chk) right (ar_subs.c:82-87); round 15 (postcondition omits the loop break when rd_skip returns 1 and the skipped listing when mod_name returns > 0) right (lines 113-124). Tally 2 right 0 wrong.

name: extract
prose: Function extract() in pax/ar_subs.c (lines 144-341; the slice 259-515 began inside it and also covered the start of wr_archive, so no function named rd_archive exists), no parameters, returns nothing. It extracts the archive members that match the patterns and options. It first calls get_arc(), (*frmt->options)(), (*frmt->st_rd)() and dir_start(), and name_start() when iflag is set; if any is negative it returns at once (the archive is left open and pat_chk is not run). Then it loops while next_head(arcn) returns 0. pat_match < 0 ends the loop. A member that does not match (pat_match > 0 or sel_chk != 0) is skipped with rd_skip(arcn->skip + arcn->pad) and the loop continues. With -u or -D the member is skipped (also via rd_skip) when the file of that name exists (lstat succeeds) and is not older, by the rules on mtime (-u), ctime (-D) or both; pat_sel or mod_name failing ends the loop, mod_name returning > 0 purges the name from the link table, skips the data and continues; the non-standard -Y/-Z flags apply the same kind of age test after the name change. With -v the name is written to listf (a full ls_list line for -vv). If the pattern has a chdname it does chdir to it (failure only warns). A member that is not a regular or contiguous file is created with lnk_creat (hard links) or node_creat, its data and padding are skipped, the name is purged from the link table if creation failed, a pending verbose line is finished, and the loop continues without restoring the directory. A regular file is created with file_creat (a negative result skips the data, purges the name and continues), its data is read with (*frmt->rd_data)(arcn, fd, &cnt), the file is closed with file_close, a pending verbose line is finished, rd_skip(cnt + arcn->pad) is called when rd_data returned 0, and if the pattern had a chdname it returns to the starting directory with fchdir(cwdfd) (failure only warns). After the loop it calls (*frmt->end_rd)(), blocks signals with sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &s_mask, NULL), ar_close(), proc_dir() (restores directory modes and times) and pat_chk().
note: Old record was dropped because the name rd_archive is not in the source; the slice is the tail of extract() (ar_subs.c:144) plus the head of wr_archive, so it is fixed under the real name extract. No reviewer claim (mechanical rejection only). The whole function was read.

name: rd_sync
prose: Function rd_sync() in pax/buf_subs.c (lines 301-355), no parameters, returns 0 or -1; it is called after a read error on an archive volume. It starts with errcnt = 0. It returns -1 immediately when maxflt == 0, and when act == APPND (after a warning). Otherwise, if ar_rdsync() returns < 0 it calls ar_next(): a failure returns -1, success sets rdcnt = 0. It then loops: ar_read(buf, blksz) returning a positive count res sets bufpt = buf, bufend = buf + res, adds res to rdcnt and returns 0. On a failed read: if maxflt > 0 it increments errcnt and, when errcnt exceeds maxflt, prints the "Archive read error limit reached" warning and goes on to ar_next(); in every other case (maxflt > 0 and the limit not yet exceeded, or maxflt < 0 where errcnt is not incremented) it calls ar_rdsync() and, if that returns 0, retries the read on the same volume (rdcnt and errcnt unchanged); otherwise it calls ar_next(): a negative result leaves the loop and returns -1, success sets rdcnt = 0 and errcnt = 0 and the loop retries.
note: Reviewers: round 1 (prose wrongly says failure when maxflt is exhausted; code may call ar_next and continue) right; round 2 (a successful ar_rdsync retries the same volume without moving to the next volume or resetting rdcnt/errcnt) right; round 15 (not every failed ar_read increments errcnt: it is skipped when maxflt < 0) right (buf_subs.c:345-352). All three describe earlier wording; the text is rewritten from the code. Tally 3 right 0 wrong.

name: buf_flush
prose: Function buf_flush(bufcnt) in pax/buf_subs.c (lines 875-982) writes the pending archive buffer to the archive in blksz blocks. bufcnt is the number of bytes in the buffer when it was called. Return values: -1 with exit_val = 1 when (a) the -R byte limit was hit (wrlimit > 0 and wrcnt > wrlimit) and ar_next() fails (wrcnt is reset to 0 first; bufpt is untouched), (b) ar_write returned 0 or a negative count and the following ar_next() fails (wrcnt reset to 0 first), or (c) a partial write left a remainder whose length is not a multiple of frmt->blkalgn (bufpt was already set to buf + remainder length before returning); 0 when, after a volume change (at the start for the byte limit, or inside the loop after a failed write and a successful ar_next), the new blksz is larger than bufcnt (bufend is reset to buf + blksz; this can happen after earlier blocks of this call were written, whose bytes are then not reported); otherwise the total number of bytes written by this call, totcnt, which may exceed bufcnt when push data are written in additional blocks. Details: after a volume change with blksz smaller than bufcnt, push = bufcnt - blksz extra bytes remain; a full block write adds blksz to wrcnt and totcnt, then moves the push bytes (copied from bufend) to the start of buf and sets bufpt = buf + push, looping again while push >= blksz; with push 0, bufpt = buf. A partial write (0 < cnt < blksz) adds cnt to totcnt and wrcnt, moves the unwritten remainder bufcnt - cnt to the start of buf, sets bufpt = buf + (bufcnt - cnt), and returns totcnt when the format has no blkalgn or the remainder is a multiple of it. So bufpt is left pointing just past the retained data (buf, buf + push, or buf + remainder), not at its start; wrcnt is increased by the bytes written and is reset to 0 whenever ar_next() is about to be called.
note: Reviewers: round 1 (omits exit_val = 1 on -1; result can exceed bufcnt when bufcnt < blksz) right; round 2 (return 0 after a volume change can happen after prior blocks were written) right (buf_subs.c:970-972); round 15 (bufpt is the end of the remainder, not its start, and is unchanged on error returns) right on the first part and partly wrong on the second: bufpt is changed before the misaligned partial-write -1 return (lines 949-955). Tally 3 right 0 wrong, 1 mixed counted within round 15. The whole function was read.

name: pax_options
prose: Static function pax_options(argc, argv) in pax/options.c (lines 179-573; the slice 302-574 showed only its middle and end, so it is not an unnamed function). It parses the pax-mode command line with getopt("ab:cdf:iklno:p:rs:tuvwx:zB:DE:G:HLOPT:U:XYZ"), sets the option globals and a local flag word flg, and exits through pax_usage() (which prints the usage text and calls exit(1)) for invalid input. Per option: a, c, d, f, i, k, l, n, r, t, u, v, w, D, H, L, O, P, X, Y, Z set their global flag (for example cflag, dflag, arcname, iflag, kflag, lflag, nflag, tflag, uflag, vflag, Dflag, Hflag, Lflag, Oflag, Xflag, Yflag, Zflag; -P clears Lflag; -z sets gzip_program = GZIP_CMD; r and w only add flags to flg); -b sets wrblksz from str_offt and calls pax_usage when it is <= 0; -o calls opt_add (failure calls pax_usage); -p scans its string and sets patime, pmtime, pids, pmode per character (a, e, m, o, p) and calls pax_usage on an invalid character; -s calls rep_add, -G grp_add, -T trng_add, -U usr_add, each failure calling pax_usage; -x looks the format up with bsearch in fsub and, if unknown, prints the known formats and calls pax_usage; -B sets wrlimit and calls pax_usage if it is <= 0 or not a multiple of BLKMULT; -E sets maxflt to -1 for the string NONE, else atoi, and calls pax_usage if negative; any other option calls pax_usage. After the loop the mode comes from flg: list sets act = LIST and listf = stdout, extract sets EXTRACT, archive ARCHIVE, append APPND, copy COPY; if no mode matches, or if flags not allowed for that mode were given (bflg nonzero, after printflg), it calls pax_usage. For ARCHIVE without -x it selects frmt = &fsub[DEFLT]. Operands are then processed by mode: LIST and EXTRACT add each as a pattern with pat_add; COPY requires a destination (else a warning and pax_usage), takes the last operand as dirptr, and falls through to ARCHIVE/APPND, which add each remaining operand with ftree_add (failure pax_usage) and then set maxflt = 0 (overriding any -E value).
note: Old record was dropped as 'unnamed options-parsing function'; the slice is inside pax_options at options.c:179, so fixed under the real name. No reviewer claim (mechanical rejection only). Whole function read; pax_usage ends in exit(1) (options.c:1547).

name: evalcommand
prose: Static function evalcommand(cmd, flags, backcmd) in sh/eval.c (lines 819-1177) executes a simple command node and returns nothing; the exit status is stored in the global exitstatus. Expansion: it sets oexitstatus = exitstatus and exitstatus = 0, initialises its own empty arglist and varlist (the caller supplies neither), expands the words, collecting leading assignments into varlist (into arglist after a declaration command), expands the redirections, computes argc and argv, and, when iflag is set, funcnest is 0 and argc > 0, remembers the last argument; with xflag it traces the command. Lookup: with no command word it uses the bltin builtin for the assignments; otherwise a PATH= assignment overrides the lookup path and clears the command hash (do_clearcmdentry = 1), and find_command / the bltin and command builtin handling (including command -p with _PATH_STDPATH, which also clears the hash, and DO_NOFUNC, which removes the special property of builtins) pick the command. Forking: if the command is an external or unknown one and (EV_EXIT is not set or traps exist), or EV_BACKCMD is set and the command is not a builtin that is safe to run in this process, it makes a job and forks (a pipe is created for EV_BACKCMD, pipe failure calls error), possibly via vforkexecshell for a plain external command without redirections or assignments in a non-interactive shell; the parent jumps to parent, the child redirects stdout for EV_BACKCMD and continues with EV_EXIT set. Execution happens in the process that continues from there, which is the child when forked: shell functions run through evaltree with shellparam, localvars, handler, funcnest and redirections saved and restored, and an exception longjmps after restoring them; builtins run with redirections pushed, output captured into memout for EV_BACKCMD (copied to backcmd->buf and nleft), stdout write errors turn a status of 0 or 1 into 2, redirections are popped (except for exec), and a caught exception is re-raised unless it is an EXERROR from a non-special builtin; external commands apply redirections, export the assignments and call shellexec, which does not return. A forked child ends with exitshell(exitstatus) after a function or builtin and never returns to the caller. The parent, for a foreground job, waits with waitforjob into exitstatus and, if interactive inside a loop and the job was signalled, sets evalskip = SKIPBREAK; for a backcmd job it stores the read pipe fd and the job in backcmd and closes the write end. At the end it sets "_" to the remembered last argument and clears the command hash again if do_clearcmdentry was set.
note: Reviewers: original (precondition wrongly requires the caller to ensure local arglist/varlist empty; code initialises them) right (eval.c:847-848); round 15 (the prose says the command may execute in the parent after forking, but it is executed in the child and the parent returns) right (eval.c:1004-1005, 1157-1170). The old prose also said the saved shell state is restored on every returning path; that holds for shell functions, and builtins restore handler, commandname, output and redirections, but external commands save nothing. Tally 2 right 0 wrong. The whole function was read.

name: setjobctl
prose: Function setjobctl(on) in sh/jobs.c (lines 171-235, compiled when JOBS is set), returns nothing. It returns immediately when on equals the current jobctl or rootshell is 0. To turn job control on it closes any previous ttyfd, opens /dev/tty (O_RDWR|O_CLOEXEC) or, if that fails, duplicates the first of descriptors 0-2 that is a tty with F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC to 10 or above, and moves ttyfd up to 10 or above if needed; any of those failing, or tcgetpgrp(ttyfd) failing, calls jobctl_notty() and returns. If the terminal's foreground process group differs from getpgrp(): without iflag it sets initialpgrp = -1, calls jobctl_notty() and returns; with iflag it sends SIGTTIN to its own process group with kill(0, SIGTTIN) and the following 'continue' only ends the do { } while (0) block, so it does not loop. It then calls setsignal for SIGTSTP, SIGTTOU and SIGTTIN, setpgid(0, rootpid), tcsetpgrp(ttyfd, rootpid) (results unchecked) and sets jobctl = on. To turn it off it does setpgid(0, initialpgrp), and, if ttyfd >= 0, tcsetpgrp(ttyfd, initialpgrp), close(ttyfd) and ttyfd = -1, calls setsignal for the same three signals and sets jobctl = on (0). jobctl_notty() closes ttyfd (setting it to -1) and then, when iflag is not set, calls setsignal for the three signals and sets jobctl = 1, returning; when iflag is set it prints "sh: can't access tty; job control turned off" and sets mflag = 0, leaving jobctl unchanged. So on the failure paths jobctl becomes 1 if iflag is clear and is unchanged if iflag is set.
note: Reviewers: original (jobctl not set to on when jobctl_notty returns with iflag) right (jobs.c:166-167); round 15 (the iflag-clear failure path sets jobctl = 1, contradicting the claim that jobctl is not set to on) right (jobs.c:159-164). The old prose also said a background shell with iflag loops on SIGTTIN instead of returning, which is wrong because of the do { } while (0) (jobs.c:202-217). Tally 2 right 0 wrong.

name: waitcmdloop
prose: Static function waitcmdloop(job) in sh/jobs.c (lines 554-608), used by the wait builtin; job is NULL (wait for any job) or a pointer to a job table entry. It loops while dowait(DOWAIT_BLOCK | DOWAIT_SIG, job) does not return -1. In each pass: if job is not NULL and job->state == JOBDONE it computes the status with getjobstatus (exit status, or WTERMSIG + 128 for a signalled job), then, if the shell is not interactive or the job's changed flag is not set, calls freejob(job); otherwise it clears job->remembered, calls deljob(job) and clears bgjob if job == bgjob; and it returns that status. If job is NULL: with njobs == 0 it returns 0; otherwise it goes over the table and, for each used job that is JOBDONE, calls freejob when not interactive or not changed, else only clears remembered (and bgjob when it is that job) without deleting it; then it looks for a job with state 0 (running) and returns 0 if there is none (so it also returns 0 when jobs exist but none is running). If a wait is still needed, dowait blocks; a return of -1 (interrupted by a signal) ends the loop, and the function sets sig = pendingsig_waitcmd, clears pendingsig_waitcmd and returns sig + 128.
note: Reviewers: original (returns 0 also when jobs exist but none are running) right (jobs.c:595-598); round 15 (for job == NULL, changed completed jobs are not freed, only their remembered flag is cleared, contradicting 'freeing every completed job') right (jobs.c:586-594). Tally 2 right 0 wrong.

name: growstrstackblock
prose: Static function growstrstackblock(n, min) in sh/memalloc.c (lines 304-308). It calls growstackblock(min) and returns stackblock() + n, a pointer n bytes into the (possibly moved) string area at the top of the shell's stack. growstackblock always enlarges that area: it raises min to at least the current stackblocksize() (stacknleft), adds stacknleft again, adds the stack-block header size, rounds the total up to a power of two of at least 512 bytes, and calls error("Out of space") when min is not below INT_MAX / 2 minus the header size. If the current stack block holds nothing yet (stacknxt equals the start of its space) it grows the block in place with ckrealloc (the address can change); otherwise it allocates a new block, copies the old string area (stacknleft bytes) into it and makes it the current block. Afterwards the string area is at least max(min, old size) + old size bytes long and its old contents are preserved at the new base, and any previous pointers into the old string area are invalid. n should not exceed the old stackblocksize() so that the returned pointer lies in the preserved data.
note: No reviewer claim. The old prose said 'ensures at least min bytes are free after the current top, growing if necessary'; the code always grows (growstackblock has no 'enough space' check) and grows by at least the old size. Checked memalloc.c:240-308.

name: growstackstr
prose: Function growstackstr() in sh/memalloc.c (lines 311-317), no parameters. It takes len = stackblocksize() (the current size of the string area at the top of the stack) and returns growstrstackblock(len, 0), that is the address len bytes into the grown string area, just past the old area's contents. It always grows the string area (by at least doubling it, possibly moving it, which invalidates pointers into it) rather than only when space is short; it is called from the STPUTC and STACKSTRNUL macros when the write pointer has reached sstrend. It does not store anything or write a NUL.
note: No reviewer claim. The old prose's 'may grow ... if there is no free space' was not what the code does (memalloc.c:241-258, 311-317).

name: makestrspace
prose: Function makestrspace(min, p) in sh/memalloc.c (lines 325-331), called from the CHECKSTRSPACE macro when fewer than min bytes remain before sstrend. It computes len = p - stackblock() and returns growstrstackblock(len, min), i.e. the address len bytes into the grown string area. Growth always happens (the macro does the space test, not this function) and is at least the old area size plus max(min, old size), so that, when p lay within the old area, at least min bytes are free after the returned pointer. The old contents are preserved at the new base, so p and other pointers into the area are invalid after the call.
note: No reviewer claim. Checked memalloc.c:241-258, 325-331 and CHECKSTRSPACE in memalloc.h:69.

name: stputbin
prose: Function stputbin(data, len, p) in sh/memalloc.c (lines 335-340) copies len bytes into the stack string area at p. It first applies CHECKSTRSPACE(len, p): if (size_t)(sstrend - p) < len, p is replaced by makestrspace(len, p) (the area is grown and may move, so any other pointers into it become invalid; data must therefore not point into that area). It then does memcpy(p, data, len) and returns p + len. No NUL byte is written. len may be 0.
note: No reviewer claim; prior prose checked and kept with the macro condition stated.

name: stputs
prose: Function stputs(data, p) in sh/memalloc.c (lines 343-346) returns stputbin(data, strlen(data), p): it appends the characters of the NUL-terminated string data (without the terminating NUL) to the stack string area at p, growing the area if needed (which may move it and invalidate other pointers into it; data must not point into it), and returns p advanced by strlen(data). No NUL is written.
note: No reviewer claim; prior prose checked.

name: xwrite
prose: Function xwrite(fd, buf, nbytes) in sh/output.c (lines 346-368) writes nbytes bytes from buf to fd, resuming after short writes. It loops on write(fd, buf, n) with n the bytes still to write. A positive result advances buf, reduces n and resets the zero-return counter ntry to 0; when n reaches 0 or less it returns nbytes. A result of 0 increments ntry, and when ntry exceeds 10 (the eleventh zero result) it returns nbytes - n, the number of bytes already written (0 when nothing was written, which is also what it returns for nbytes == 0). A negative result with errno EINTR is retried without changing ntry or n, so the eleven zero results need not be consecutive; any other negative result returns -1 with errno set by write. The buffer and descriptor stay with the caller.
note: Reviewers: round 2 (for nbytes = 0 the zero-write return is 0, not between 0 and nbytes - 1) right for that edge case; round 15 (ntry is not reset on EINTR, so the eleven zero returns need not be consecutive) right (output.c:355-367); the old prose said 'consecutive'. Tally 2 right 0 wrong.

name: redirect
prose: Function redirect(redir, flags) in sh/redir.c (lines 103-161), returns nothing; flags may contain REDIR_PUSH and REDIR_BACKQ. It starts with INTOFF, clears a 10-entry array memory[] and sets memory[1] to flags & REDIR_BACKQ. With REDIR_PUSH it increments empty_redirs; if redir is non-NULL it also allocates a redirtab with ckmalloc, marks its renamed[] entries EMPTY, saves fd0_redirected and the earlier empty count in it, chains it onto redirlist and resets empty_redirs to 0. For each redirection node it records fd0_redirected = 1 for fd 0 and skips (continue) a dup of a descriptor onto itself (NTOFD or NFROMFD with dupfd equal to fd). Otherwise, with REDIR_PUSH and the fd not yet saved in this redirtab, it dups the fd to a descriptor >= 10 with F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC (EBADF is recorded as CLOSED, any other error calls INTON and error()), and then calls openredirect(n, memory), which opens the file or duplicates the descriptor and may call error() on failure (error does not return). After each applied redirection it executes INTON and then INTOFF again, so interrupts are re-enabled between redirections. At the end it sets out1 to &memout when memory[1] is still set and out2 to &memout when memory[2] is set (a file or dup redirection of that descriptor clears or sets the memory flag), and executes INTON.
note: Reviewers: original (omits the REDIR_BACKQ memory redirection; not every redirection is applied to its fd) right (redir.c:114, 132-134, 156-159); round 15 (interrupts are re-enabled after each redirection, not suppressed for the whole operation) right (redir.c:152-154). Tally 2 right 0 wrong. I read openredirect only for its failure behaviour (lines 165-214).

name: static const char *ccval(struct cchar *p, int c)
prose: Function ccval(p, c) in stty/print.c (lines 251-280; the slice began in the middle, and no function named format_control_char exists). It returns a pointer to a static 5-byte buffer buf (shared by all calls, overwritten by the next call, not a caller buffer) or to the string literal "<undef>". If p->sub is VMIN or VTIME it writes the decimal value of c into buf with snprintf (truncated to 4 digits plus NUL if longer) and returns buf. Otherwise, if c equals _POSIX_VDISABLE it returns the literal "<undef>". Otherwise it builds the text in buf: if bit 0200 of c is set it writes "M-" and clears that bit; then for c == 0177 it writes "^?", for c < 040 it writes '^' followed by c + '@', and otherwise it writes c itself; it appends the NUL and returns buf. The longest result, "M-^?" or "M-^X" style, is 4 characters plus the NUL.
note: Old record was dropped (the name in it, format_control_char, is not in the source); the real function is ccval at print.c:251, so it is fixed under that name. The old prose said buf is a caller-supplied buffer; it is a function-static buffer (print.c:253). No reviewer claim (mechanical rejection only).

name: main
prose: main(argc, argv) of timeout.c (lines 268-499). It parses options with getopt_long("+fhk:ps:v"): -f foreground, -k sets do_second_kill and parses the duration with parse_duration, -p preserve, -s converts the signal with str2sig (failure calls errx(EXIT_INVALID, ...)), -v verbose; any other result, including -h, calls usage(), which exits with EXIT_FAILURE; with fewer than 2 remaining arguments it also calls usage(). parse_duration exits with EXIT_INVALID for a bad duration. Unless -f is set it acquires a reaper with procctl(PROC_REAP_ACQUIRE) (failure exits with EXIT_FAILURE). It blocks all signals (failure EXIT_FAILURE), creates a control pipe with pipe2 (failure EXIT_FAILURE) and forks (failure EXIT_FAILURE). The child restores the signal disposition of killsig and the old signal mask, reads one byte from the pipe (an error or EOF exits with EXIT_FAILURE), and calls execvp; if exec fails it warns and calls _exit(127) for ENOENT and _exit(126) otherwise. The parent installs sig_handler for all catchable signals (SIGTTIN and SIGTTOU are ignored; a failure exits with EXIT_FAILURE), starts the timer with set_interval(first_kill) (setitimer failure exits), writes one byte to the pipe (error or short write exits with EXIT_FAILURE) and loops with sigsuspend: on SIGCHLD it collects children with waitid(WNOHANG), recording the target child's status in child_si and finishing the loop when it is done (and, unless -f, when the reaper has no children left); on the alarm or a terminating signal it sends the signal to the child (killsig on timeout, setting timedout), arming the second timer and switching killsig to SIGKILL when -k was given; any other caught signal is forwarded. After the loop it releases the reaper unless -f. It then returns EXIT_TIMEOUT (124) when the timer fired and -p was not given; otherwise, if the child was killed or dumped, it calls kill_self(child_si.si_status), which disables core dumps, resets the disposition and raises that signal on itself and does not return (if raise fails it calls err(128 + signo)); otherwise it returns the child's exit status when it exited normally, or EXIT_FAILURE for any other termination code.
note: Reviewers: original (omits the fallback EXIT_FAILURE return for other child_si.si_code values) right (timeout.c:494-495, and the old prose actually already had it); round 15 (the fatal child signal is re-raised only when it did not time out without --preserve-status, contrary to the unconditional claim) right (timeout.c:486-490: the EXIT_TIMEOUT branch is tested first). Tally 2 right 0 wrong. The whole function was read.

name: dtrace_aggregate_walk_joined
prose: Function dtrace_aggregate_walk_joined(dtp, aggvars, naggvars, func, arg) in libdtrace/dt_aggregate.c (lines 1686-2126; the slice 1768-2021 was the middle of it, so it is not an unnamed function). It calls func once for each distinct key (tuple) found in the consumed aggregation data, passing an array of naggvars + 1 pointers to dtrace_aggdata_t: element 0 is the representative key entry, elements 1..naggvars are the data for the aggregation variables in the order of aggvars (rotated back by the DTRACEOPT_AGGSORTPOS option, which is taken as 0 when unset or not below naggvars). Failure and special returns: if any aggvars entry is DTRACE_AGGVARIDNONE or negative it returns dt_set_errno(dtp, EDT_BADAGGVAR); allocation failures (the id-to-position map, the zero-filled entries, the remap, the zero data buffers, the sorted array or a bundle) return -1 after freeing what it allocated; if no aggregation entry matches any of aggvars it returns 0 without calling func; if func returns -1 it stops and returns -1; otherwise it returns 0 after the last bundle. It builds a map from variable id to position (duplicate variable ids are handled through a remap), makes a zero-filled placeholder entry for each variable (taking sizes from the first entry seen, from the aggregation descriptors, or, for an anonymous enabling, from the first non-empty one, and storing the variable id and, for lquantize(), its parameters in it), collects all matching hash entries into a sorted array, sorts it with dt_aggregate_keyvarcmp while holding dt_qsort_lock, groups entries with equal keys into bundles (variables missing for a key use the zero-filled placeholder or the remapped entry), sorts the bundles with dt_aggregate_bundlecmp, and releases the lock before calling func. At the end (success or failure after allocation) it frees the bundles, the zero-filled data, zaggdata, sorted, remap and map.
note: Old record was dropped as an unnamed enclosing function. The slice is the middle of dtrace_aggregate_walk_joined (dt_aggregate.c:1686); fixed under the real name. No reviewer claim (mechanical rejection only). The whole function was read (about 440 lines).

name: dt_as
prose: Function dt_as(pcb) in libdtrace/dt_as.c (lines 209-503) assembles the instruction list pcb->pcb_ir into a newly allocated dtrace_difo_t and returns it; the caller owns it. pcb->pcb_difo must be NULL on entry (assert). It selects relocation masks from pcb->pcb_hdl->dt_linkmode (kernel, primary, dynamic or static); any other link mode calls xyerror(D_UNKNOWN, ...). It allocates the DIFO, its instruction buffer and a label table (any allocation failure does longjmp(pcb->pcb_jmpbuf, EDT_NOMEM)). Pass one copies the instructions (skipping labelled nops), records label positions and counts kernel relocations, user relocations and xlate references; an instruction with an extern that is not SETX, XLATE or XLARG calls xyerror(D_UNKNOWN, "unexpected assembler relocation ..."). Pass two sets dtdo_destructive for calls to the copyout and copyoutstr subroutines and rewrites each branch with its label's index. The label table is freed. It then allocates and fills the variable table from the tls, global and local identifier hashes, then the kernel, user and xlate relocation tables (each failure longjmps with EDT_NOMEM). In the third pass, for each relocation: xlate entries go to dt_as_xlate; for SETX the symbol is classified by the masks, and unless the matching DTRACE_C_KNODEF or DTRACE_C_UNODEF flag is set dt_as_undef calls xyerror(D_ASRELO, "relocation remains against ... symbol"); the symbol name is inserted into the string table (failure longjmps with EDT_NOMEM, an offset above DIF_STROFF_MAX longjmps with EDT_STR2BIG) and the relocation descriptor is filled. It then copies the string table and the integer table into the DIFO (allocation failures longjmp with EDT_NOMEM), sets dtdo_rtype from pcb->pcb_dret with dt_node_diftype, clears pcb->pcb_difo and pcb->pcb_dret, disassembles to stderr when DTRACE_C_DIFV is set, and returns the DIFO. On any of the error exits pcb->pcb_difo is left pointing at the partly built DIFO.
note: Reviewer round 15 (omits the xyerror longjmp for an unexpected relocation opcode) right (dt_as.c:309-311); the old prose also omitted the invalid link mode and the D_ASRELO 'relocation remains' error (dt_as.c:204, 262, 440-441). Tally 1 right 0 wrong. The whole function was read; xyerror is assumed to leave the function without returning (it is used as an error exit throughout).

name: dt_compile_agg
prose: Static function dt_compile_agg(dtp, dnp, sdp) in libdtrace/dt_cc.c (lines 1193-1599; the slice 1268-1519 was the middle of it, so dt_action_quantize is not a function in this file), returns nothing. It compiles the actions for a statement of the form @agg[tuple] = func(args). Compile errors are reported with dnerror (an error exit, not a return). If the aggregation has no aggregating function (dn_aggfun NULL) it reports D_AGG_NULL; if the function's first argument exists and is not scalar it reports D_AGG_SCALAR. It records the aggregation id as the first tuple element (an action created with dt_stmt_action and dt_action_difconst), then for each tuple element creates an action and counts n: stack and ustack/jstack elements use dt_action_stack_args and dt_action_ustack_args, uaddr, usym, umod, sym and mod elements use dt_action_symmod_args, and any other element is generated with dt_cg and assembled with dt_as into a DIFEXPR action. For lquantize() it requires argument 1 and 2 to be integer constants within 32 bits with limit >= base, the optional step (argument 3) to be a positive 16-bit constant, at least one and at most 65535 levels ((limit - base) / step), builds the packed argument, stores it as the aggregation's dis_auxinfo the first time and otherwise reports a D_LQUANT_MATCH* error if it differs from the earlier use, and sets incr (the optional increment argument) and argmax = 5. For llquantize() it checks the factor, low, high and steps arguments (integer constants within 16 bits, factor >= 2, low < high, steps >= factor, divisibility rules, no overflow of the order), packs and compares them with dis_auxinfo the same way, and sets incr and argmax = 6. For quantize() it sets incr to the second argument and argmax = 2. If an increment expression exists it must be scalar and the last argument (otherwise a compile error is reported), and it gets its own DIFEXPR action with void return type and n is incremented. Finally it asserts sdp->dtsd_aggdata is NULL, stores the aggregation identifier there, creates the aggregating action with dtad_kind = the function id, dtad_ntuple = n and dtad_arg = the packed argument (0 for the other functions) and, when the function has arguments, generates and assembles the first argument into the action's DIFO.
note: Old record was dropped with an empty prose because the name dt_action_quantize is not in the source; the slice is the middle of dt_compile_agg (dt_cc.c:1193), so fixed under the real name. No reviewer claim (mechanical rejection only). I read lines 1193-1599 but, for the error-message lines of the llquantize checks, only the conditions (not every message text). The error tags of the increment-argument checks (lines 1558-1574) were not recorded in the prose, only that the checks exist.

name: dt_scope_pop
prose: Function dt_scope_pop() in libdtrace/dt_decl.c (lines 1103-1129), no parameters, returns the restored declaration pointer. It takes the root scope rsp = &yypcb->pcb_dstack and dsp = rsp->ds_next. If dsp is NULL it does longjmp(yypcb->pcb_jmpbuf, EDT_NOSCOPE). If dsp->ds_ctfp is non-NULL it calls ctf_update(dsp->ds_ctfp); a CTF_ERR result calls xyerror(D_UNKNOWN, "failed to update type definitions: ...") and does not return. When ds_ctfp is NULL, or ctf_update succeeded, it then frees the root's current declaration (dt_decl_free(rsp->ds_decl)) and ds_ident, copies the saved scope's ds_decl, ds_next, ds_ident, ds_ctfp, ds_type, ds_class and ds_enumval into the root, frees the saved scope node dsp and returns rsp->ds_decl (the restored declaration, which may be NULL).
note: Reviewers: original (requires ds_next non-NULL, longjmp EDT_NOSCOPE; omits the ctf_update side effect) right; round 15 (the free and restore happen regardless of ds_ctfp and whenever ctf_update did not fail, not only in an 'otherwise' branch) right (dt_decl.c:1111-1128). The old prose treated the ctf_update branch and the restore as alternatives. Tally 2 right 0 wrong.

name: dt_decl_member
prose: Function dt_decl_member(dnp) in libdtrace/dt_decl.c (lines 504-647); dnp is the optional bit-field width node, and the member name, if any, is in yypcb->pcb_dstack.ds_ident. It returns nothing. It takes the enclosing scope dsp = pcb_dstack.ds_next and the pending declaration ddp = pcb_dstack.ds_decl. Exits by longjmp(yypcb->pcb_jmpbuf, ...): EDT_NOSCOPE when there is no scope, EDT_NODECL when there is no declaration, EDT_COMPILER when dt_decl_type fails. Exits by xyerror (compile error, no return): D_DECL_MNAME when there is neither a width node nor a name; D_DECL_SCOPE when the name contains a backquote; D_DECL_DYNOBJ for a member of the dynamic type; D_DECL_INCOMPLETE for a forward declaration or a struct/union of size 0; D_DECL_VOIDOBJ for a member of size 0; and, for a bit-field, D_DECL_BFCONST (width is not a positive integral constant), D_DECL_BFTYPE (base type not a non-void integer), D_DECL_BFSIZE (width greater than the type's bits), and D_UNKNOWN for failures of ctf_add_integer or ctf_update, of ctf_add_type (copying the member type into the scope's container) and of ctf_add_member. If the declaration has no kind and no name it first defaults to an integer type. With a width node it cooks the node; an anonymous zero-width bit-field (no name and a constant 0) frees the node and skips adding any member; otherwise it creates a new integer type of the given number of bits in the scope's container. If the member type lives in neither the scope's container nor its parent it copies it into the scope's container. It then adds the member with ctf_add_member. On every normal return (member added or the zero-width case) it frees the name, sets ds_ident to NULL and calls dt_decl_reset().
note: Reviewer round 15 (EDT_NOSCOPE, EDT_NODECL and EDT_COMPILER use longjmp, not xyerror) right (dt_decl.c:519-534); the old prose attributed all failures to xyerror. Tally 1 right 0 wrong. The whole function was read.

name: dt_node_decl
prose: Function dt_node_decl() in libdtrace/dt_parser.c (lines 1436-1776; the slice 1531-1782 was its second half, so dt_decl_id is not its name), no parameters, always returns NULL when it returns. It takes the pending declaration ddp = dt_decl_top() and the root scope dsp = &yypcb->pcb_dstack, and resolves the type with dt_decl_type (failure longjmps with EDT_COMPILER). With no identifier (dsp->ds_ident NULL): a declaration that is not a struct, union or enum is a D_DECL_USELESS error, otherwise it just logs and returns NULL. A backquote in the identifier is a D_DECL_SCOPE error. A function type with the default or static class becomes extern. Then by storage class: auto, register and static are errors (D_DECL_BADCLASS); extern checks whether the symbol exists in the chosen module (D_DECL_IDRED if the types differ, D_UNKNOWN if dt_module_extern fails); typedef rejects a name that is already a global identifier or an existing CTF type (D_DECL_IDRED), copies the source type into the module's container if needed (D_UNKNOWN on failure) and adds the typedef; the remaining classes (this, self, default) declare a variable: array declarations without a dimension or tuple signature are D_DECL_ARRNULL, redeclaring a built-in identifier or a typedef name is D_DECL_IDRED, associative arrays cannot be 'this' variables (D_DECL_LOCASSC); an existing identifier with a different kind, type, tuple length or key type is D_DECL_IDRED; for a new identifier, void objects and incomplete struct/union types are rejected (D_DECL_VOIDOBJ, D_DECL_INCOMPLETE), the next id is taken (D_ID_OFLOW if exhausted), the identifier is inserted in the thread-local, local or global hash with its type (EDT_NOMEM longjmp if insertion fails) and, for associative arrays, its signature is cooked. At the end of every non-error path it frees ds_ident and sets it to NULL and returns NULL. All the error tags are compile errors raised with xyerror (no return).
note: Old record was still-rejected (name dt_decl_id not in the file); the slice is the second half of dt_node_decl (dt_parser.c:1436), so it is fixed under that name. No reviewer claim (mechanical rejections only). The whole function was read.

name: dt_node_op2
prose: Function dt_node_op2(op, lp, rp) in libdtrace/dt_parser.c (lines 1970-2139); lp and rp are non-NULL nodes. First, if rp is an integer constant 0 and op is DT_TOK_MOD, DT_TOK_DIV, DT_TOK_MOD_EQ or DT_TOK_DIV_EQ, it calls xyerror(D_DIV_ZERO, ...) (no return); this check happens before any folding, so the folded division or modulo below never divides by zero. If both lp and rp are integer constants it allocates an integer node (dt_node_int(0)) and, for op in logical or (LOR), logical xor, logical and, BOR, XOR, BAND, EQU, NEQ, LT, LE, GT, GE, LSH, RSH, ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV and MOD, computes the result with the promoted type for the arithmetic, bitwise and relational operators (signed comparison, division and modulo when the promoted type is signed), the plain int type for the logical, equality and relational results, and the type of lp for shifts (the shift count is not range-checked); for any other op it frees the new node and continues. When folding succeeded it frees lp and rp and returns the new integer node. Otherwise, if op is DT_TOK_LPAR (a cast), rp is an integer constant and lp has integer type, it adjusts rp's value to the target size and signedness with dt_cast, gives rp the type and merged attributes of lp, frees lp and returns rp itself. In every other case it allocates a new DT_NODE_OP2 node with dn_op = op, dn_left = lp and dn_right = rp (the new node takes ownership of both) and returns it. It never returns NULL; allocation failure longjmps with EDT_NOMEM (inside dt_node_alloc) and the divide-by-zero check exits through xyerror.
note: Reviewer round 15 (the DIV/MOD cases divide by r without a zero check, so the annotation about xyerror/longjmp on constant zero is wrong) wrong: the zero check is at the top of the function (dt_parser.c:1979-1982) and covers exactly the constant-zero right operand that the folding would otherwise divide by. The slice 2084-2334 began in the middle of this function (it ended at line 2139), so the whole function was read from 1970. Tally 0 right 1 wrong.

name: dt_pragma_line
prose: Static function dt_pragma_line(prname, dnp) in libdtrace/dt_pragma.c (lines 448-490), returns nothing; it handles a #line or #pragma line directive. It takes fnp = dnp->dn_list and inp = fnp->dn_list (each only if the previous exists). It raises xyerror(D_PRAGMA_MALFORM, ...) (no return) when dnp is NULL or not a DT_NODE_INT, when fnp exists and is not a DT_NODE_STRING, or when inp exists and is not a DT_NODE_INT; nodes after inp are ignored and not checked. If fnp exists it frees the old yypcb->pcb_filetag and then, unless the file name begins with "/dev/fd/", stores fnp->dn_string in pcb_filetag and sets fnp->dn_string to NULL; for a name beginning with "/dev/fd/" it sets pcb_filetag to NULL and leaves fnp->dn_string in place. Without fnp, pcb_filetag is unchanged. If inp exists, pcb_idepth is incremented when its value is 1 and decremented when its value is 2 and pcb_idepth is nonzero; other values change nothing. Finally it sets yylineno = dnp->dn_value.
note: Reviewers: original (pcb_filetag is not always swapped: /dev/fd clears it and an absent file leaves it unchanged) right; round 15 (extra nodes after the state token are ignored, not rejected by xyerror) right (dt_pragma.c:453-458, 482-487). The old prose already had the /dev/fd and unchanged cases but said any other shape makes xyerror abort. Tally 2 right 0 wrong.
